entry.title: Why You Should Be Wary of Texas SB 2420’s Age-Verification Push
entry.content:
Texas just enacted SB 2420, the “App Store Accountability Act,” which imposes age-verification and parental-consent duties on app stores and developers. On paper, the goal is to protect kids. In practice, it creates large new targets of sensitive identity data and forces workflows that many orgs are not prepared to defend.

This post unpacks what SB 2420 actually requires, how it interacts with other Texas age-verification laws, and what it means for organizations that care about security and PII hygiene.

What SB 2420 does

SB 2420 adds Chapter 121 to the Texas Business and Commerce Code

Highlights:

  • Creates mandatory age-verification for app stores and developers, along with parental consent for minor accounts. The law defines “age categories,” assigns them at the app-store level, and expects developers to verify the category for each user and whether parental consent exists for minors (bill analysis; Apple developer update).
  • Ties the verification system to app-store provided data and prescribes compliance hooks, violations, and enforcement under Texas deceptive trade practices.
  • Applies beyond the narrow category of adult content. SB 2420 regulates general app distribution and developer obligations, not just pornography sites (Legislative tracking summary).

Separate from SB 2420, Texas also has a pornography-site age-verification law that the U.S. Supreme Court allowed to stand in June 2025, shaping a judiciary more willing to uphold aggressive age checks (additional coverage).

Tech platforms have already indicated they will comply with SB 2420, while warning about privacy and safety risks of doing so at scale.

The cybersecurity and PII problem

From a defender’s perspective, SB 2420 pushes the ecosystem toward identity-heavy gating for activities that were previously pseudonymous or low-friction. That shift has specific risks:

  1. Bigger breach blast radius
    Centralized age-verification databases are catnip for attackers. If your workflow collects government IDs, selfies, or facial embeddings to “prove adulthood,” you have created a high-value identity store. A compromise means durable identity theft, not just password resets (OWASP: Sensitive Data; FTC: Retain only what you need).

  2. Linkability and tracking
    When an app store’s age category becomes the upstream truth and developers must verify against it, the resulting identifiers and consent tokens can be used to correlate activity across apps unless carefully designed with privacy-preserving tokens (W3C Verifiable Credentials overview; VC Data Model 2.0).

  3. Fishing for phishers
    “Upload your ID to continue” is a phisher’s dream. Any statewide push that normalizes ID submission online will increase convincing phishing and MFA-fatigue style attacks targeting parents and teens (Cofense: ID & selfie phishing).

  4. Shadow retention
    Even when teams intend to “verify and delete,” ad-hoc logs, analytics events, debug screenshots, crash dumps, and vendor mirrors tend to quietly retain artifacts. That undermines data-minimization claims and expands incident-response scope (OWASP Logging CS; OWASP ASVS §7.1).

  5. Vendor risk and legal coupling
    SB 2420 intertwines app stores, age-assurance vendors, and developers. Each additional party brings new attack surface, new SOC maturity assumptions, and new breach notification paths, all under enforcement theories like deceptive trade practices (bill analysis; NIST Privacy Framework).

Practical guidance: how to comply without torching privacy

If you must support Texas users, design like an adversary is watching.

  • Prefer possession-based age proofs over data hoarding. Use on-device age tokens or selective-disclosure credentials so your system learns only “over 18” or “parental consent present,” not the date of birth or ID number. Think W3C verifiable credentials or ISO mobile driver’s license style selective-disclosure, with unlinkable, per-relying-party tokens (W3C VCs; Bellovin on limits; New America brief).
  • Zero-retention by default. If policy or vendor forces ID checks, hash and immediately discard raw images. Prove eligibility, store only a short-lived, scoped token, and keep a separate audit trail that shows “a compliant check happened” without storing PII (FTC data minimization; FPF data minimization paper).
  • Kill implicit logging. Disable verbose logs during verification, scrub PII from exceptions, and put log scrubbing in CI. Make “no PII in logs” a test, not a wish (OWASP Logging CS; ASVS controls).
  • Vendor containment. If you onboard an age-assurance provider, insist on: DPIA/TRA, data-flow diagrams, encryption posture, penetration-test reports, data-deletion SLAs, and incident-response integration (NIST Privacy Framework).
  • Threat model the consent loop. Assume attackers will impersonate parents. Require out-of-band parental confirmation and rate-limit consent flows (Cofense example).
  • Transparency reports. Publish aggregate stats on verification volumes, failures, and deletion latency. The sunlight disciplines your own retention and provides evidence of good-faith privacy engineering (NIST Privacy Framework).
  • Plan for circumvention. Users will VPN or sideload to dodge friction. Keep security controls proportional and avoid collecting more data than the attacker would surrender to a non-compliant alternative.

My take as a security practitioner

The security goal is legitimate. The implementation vector is risky. By driving the market toward identity proofs for everyday app use, SB 2420 increases the amount of sensitive data that must exist, then asks a fragmented ecosystem to protect it indefinitely. That is not where you want your breach exposure.

Could we do age assurance with privacy-preserving design? Yes. But that requires strict data minimization, unlinkable tokens, verifiable deletion, and third-party audits. Most orgs are not there yet, and many vendors still monetize the very signals we need to minimize.

Bottom line: be wary. If you operate in Texas, implement the thinnest possible verification that satisfies the statute. Avoid collecting real IDs unless you have no alternative, and if you must, do it through a provider that supports selective disclosure and immediate deletion. Treat every new field you collect as a future data-breach headline, because that is how attackers will treat it.

For policy folks tracking the bigger picture

SB 2420 lands in a legal environment that is increasingly comfortable with age checks, as the Supreme Court’s Texas pornography-site ruling showed this summer (more coverage). That momentum will encourage more states to follow. Meanwhile, trade associations are challenging SB 2420 on First Amendment and overbreadth grounds, and large platforms are warning about “real privacy and safety risks” as they implement.

Security teams should plan for multi-state divergence, adopt portable privacy architectures, and assume further mandates on parental dashboards, feature gating, and data-broker suppression are coming. Build the privacy-preserving plumbing now so you are not forced into emergency identity collection later.

References

  1. Texas SB 2420 (App Store Accountability Act), enrolled text (PDF): https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/pdf/SB02420F.pdf
  2. Texas Business & Commerce Code, Chapter 121 (as amended by SB 2420): https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/pdf/SB02420F.pdf
  3. Committee Bill Analysis for C.S.S.B. 2420: https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/analysis/html/SB02420H.HTM
  4. Summary of SB 2420 scope and sponsors (LegiScan): https://legiscan.com/TX/bill/SB2420/2025
  5. Supreme Court action regarding Texas pornography-site age-verification law (June 27, 2025) — Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-supreme-court-poised-rule-challenge-texas-age-check-online-porn-2025-06-27/
  6. National reporting on age-verification trends following the Texas ruling — AP News: https://apnews.com/article/12a73197796fe8c4bef0d888259543cf
  7. Coverage of platform compliance statements and privacy-risk concerns — Apple Developer News: https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=btkirlj8
  8. OWASP Top 10 (Sensitive Data Exposure) — guidance on minimizing stored sensitive data: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2017/A3_2017-Sensitive_Data_Exposure

entry.title: Responding to NIST’s 2025 Password Standard Update (SP 800-63B-4)
entry.content:
This article covers the changes in NIST’s July 2025 revision of the Digital Identity Guidelines for authentication (SP 800-63B-4), why they matter, and how to update your policies and controls accordingly. It is aimed at security leaders, IT teams, and MSPs who manage authentication for users.

I have read it so you don’t have to. Here are the key takeaways and action items.

NIST finalized the 2025 revision of the Digital Identity Guidelines for authentication, SP 800-63B-4. The headline is simple: length and screening beat complexity rules, forced resets are out unless there is evidence of compromise, and the experience must support password managers and modern character sets. NIST also states clearly that passwords are not phishing-resistant, so they are a floor, not the ceiling, of your authentication strategy.[1]

What changed in 2025

NIST tightened and clarified several requirements and reorganized the presentation. The big shifts you should act on now:

  • Minimum length

    • Passwords used as the only factor must be at least 15 characters.
    • Passwords used only as one factor in MFA may be shorter but must be at least 8 characters.[1:1]

  • Maximum length and character acceptance

    • Verifiers should permit at least 64 characters.
    • Accept all printing ASCII characters plus spaces, and NIST recommends accepting Unicode; count each Unicode code point as a single character.[1:2]

  • No composition rules

    • Do not require mixtures of character types. Replace brittle complexity rules with smarter screening and rate limiting.[1:3]

  • No arbitrary periodic resets

    • Do not force periodic password changes. Require a change only when there is evidence of compromise or upon user request.[1:4]

  • Blocklist screening is mandatory

    • Screen new passwords against a blocklist that includes breach corpuses, dictionary words, and context-specific terms such as the service name and username derivatives. Reject and explain why.[1:5]

  • Support password managers and usability

    • Allow paste and autofill. Offer a show-password option. Normalize Unicode before hashing if accepted.[1:6]

  • Storage and verification

  • Use salted, modern password hashing with tunable work factors, and keep versioning metadata so you can migrate safely later.[2]

Why this matters

Short minimums, quirky composition rules, blocked paste, and monthly resets train users into predictable behavior and make defenders chase noise. Attackers exploit those patterns. The 2025 guidance centers controls on the math that matters: longer secrets, denial of weak choices, and throttling that makes online guessing expensive. It also aligns UX with real behavior through managers, passphrases, and Unicode acceptance.[1:7]

Policy text you can adopt today

Use language like the following to align with SP 800-63B-4:

  1. Length

    • Single-factor passwords must be 15+ characters.
    • Passwords used only as one factor in MFA must be 8+ characters.[1:8]

  2. Acceptance

    • Permit ≥64 characters; accept all printing ASCII and spaces.
    • Accept Unicode; count by code point.[1:9]

  3. Creation rules

    • Do not impose character class requirements.
    • Do not use password hints or knowledge-based questions.[1:10]

  4. Screening

    • Compare proposed passwords against a blocklist of commonly used, expected, or compromised values. Provide actionable feedback on rejection.[1:11]

  5. Reset policy

    • No periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise, or the user requests it.[1:12]

  6. UX and managers

    • Permit paste and autofill. Provide a show-password toggle. Normalize Unicode before hashing.[1:13]

  7. Rate limiting

    • Throttle failed attempts per account with sensible lockout and messaging. Follow the verifier controls in Section 3.[1:14]

  8. Storage

    • Hash with a modern algorithm and unique salt; record algorithm and parameters for future migration.[2:1]

Engineering checklist

  • Enrollment and change flows

    • Add a breach-corpus screen to every new or changed password. Combine with rate limiting.[1:15]

  • Input controls

    • Enable paste and autofill. Add a show-password control. Avoid truncation. Accept spaces and do not strip intended Unicode.[1:16]

  • Normalization

    • If Unicode is accepted, apply NFC normalization before hashing.[1:17]

  • Hashing

    • Use a modern password hashing scheme with strong, tunable cost factors and unique per-secret salts. Track parameters to raise costs over time.[2:2]

  • Abuse controls

    • Enforce attempt throttling per account. Keep error messages non-revealing.[1:18]

Strategy for leaders

  1. Treat passwords as a legacy factor

    • Passwords are not phishing-resistant. Raise the bar with phishing-resistant authenticators such as passkeys and FIDO2 security keys for material risk, while keeping passwords to reduce support friction where needed.[1:19]

  2. Make policy humane

    • Replace composition rules and arbitrary rotation with screening, length, and throttling. Users respond to friction by choosing predictable patterns. The 2025 model is designed to break those patterns.[1:20]

  3. Instrument the pipeline

    • Log password creation outcomes, rejection reasons, and throttling events. Use the telemetry to tune blocklists and cost factors.

  4. Roll out in phases

    • Phase 1: Enable paste, show-password, and Unicode acceptance.
    • Phase 2: Add breach screening and rate limiting.
    • Phase 3: Raise minimums to 15 for single-factor flows, keep 8 for MFA-only flows.
    • Phase 4: Move priority populations to phishing-resistant authenticators.

Frequently asked questions

Do we really have to allow 64 characters and spaces?
NIST’s usability and security guidance calls for at least 64, allows spaces, and recommends accepting Unicode. This supports passphrases and password managers.[1:21]

Can we still require a number and a special character?
No. Composition rules are out. Use a blocklist and length requirements instead.[1:22]

What about quarterly password changes?
Stop doing that unless there is evidence of compromise. That is explicit in the new text.[1:23]

Are passwords enough if we screen and throttle correctly?
They reduce risk when done right, but they are not phishing-resistant. Use phishing-resistant MFA for accounts with meaningful privileges or sensitive data.[1:24]

Footnotes

  1. NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (final, July 2025). Online HTML reference with normative requirements for password length, composition, screening, resets, Unicode, and usability: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html. ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎

  2. NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (final, July 2025). PDF for archival citation: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-63B-4.pdf. ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎

entry.title: Introducing my new CybersecKyle Security How-To Series: the full roadmap
entry.content:
This will be the home base for my new CybersecKyle Security How-To Series. It is a library of practical guides. Each guide ships a small download and a quick way to prove your changes worked.

This roadmap is a working plan. I will adjust as I go, based on feedback along the way. My goal is to make security skills approachable, useful, and even fun.

Each part will link to its own post with full details, steps, and downloads. Continue to check back here or subscribe to the RSS feed for updates.

I will also post updates on my Mastodon with hashtags, #CybersecKyleHowTo and the track tag, e.g. #EverydayDefense.

How this works

  • Guides are grouped into tracks, I call them seasons.
  • Posts use clear steps, plain language, and a validation section.

  4. From findings to fixes with a short report

What you can expect

  • Clear steps you can finish in one sitting
  • A tangible download every time
  • A quick validation so you know it worked

entry.title: CybersecKyle Security How-To Series: Everyday Defense, Part 1 - Password Managers + MFA
entry.content:
This article is part of the CybersecKyle Security How-To Series, a step-by-step collection that starts with everyday safety and ramps up to blue team skills. New to the series? Start here.

Why this matters

Most breaches start with weak or reused passwords. A password manager creates one strong vault to generate and store unique logins. Multi factor authentication (MFA) adds a second check so a stolen password alone is not enough. The goal is fewer logins in your head, stronger logins on every site, and a plan that prevents lockouts.

What you will build

  • A password manager that holds your logins and generates new ones
  • MFA on your most important accounts
  • A small recovery kit that you can store safely

Key terms in plain language

  • Password manager: An app that stores and fills logins. Good ones encrypt on your device before sync.
  • TOTP: A six digit code that refreshes every 30 seconds. Works offline.
  • Hardware key: A small USB or NFC device that proves you are you. Phishing resistant.
  • Backup codes: One time codes that let you in if your phone or key is missing.

What to choose

Pick one manager you will use daily. I suggest Proton Pass(you can get 60% off right now for their Black Friday deal) as a strong, privacy-focused option. I use Proton’s apps myself, and absolutely recommend them for personal and family use.

Other Password Managers like Bitwarden, 1Password, or iCloud Keychain are all solid as well. The best choice is the one you will open every day on every device. Decide once and commit.

Risks and how we reduce them

  • Lockout risk: We set at least two factors and store backup codes in the vault item.
  • Phishing risk: We prefer TOTP or a hardware key over SMS.
  • Data loss risk: We keep a written master passphrase in a sealed envelope.

Prerequisites

  • Your computer and your phone
  • About 60 to 90 minutes the first time

Steps

  1. Install and secure the manager
    Install the desktop app, the browser extension, and the phone app. Create your account. Set a long master passphrase made from at least 20 characters (use a mix of letters, numbers, and symbols).

  2. Turn on MFA for the manager
    Open your account security page. Enable TOTP or a hardware key. Enroll at least two factors. Phone plus a spare hardware key is ideal.

  3. Import what you already have
    Export passwords from your old browser or manager as CSV. Import into the new manager. Run the health check to find weak, reused, or breached passwords.

  4. Clean up and strengthen
    Merge duplicates. Remove stale entries. For any reused password, generate a unique one and update the site. Start with the most important accounts.

  5. Enable MFA on the top ten
    Email, bank, cloud storage, social, phone carrier, domain registrar, your password manager, Apple or Google account. Prefer TOTP or a hardware key. Avoid SMS if you can. Save backup codes in the item’s secure notes.

  6. Build a recovery kit
    Store you master password somewhere safe and secure (I keep mine in Apple Note and lock it). Add a second factor on a different device or a second hardware key. Store the spare key away from home. Document a trusted contact if you want that safety net.

Validate your work

  • Sign out of the manager on your desktop and sign back in with MFA.
  • On your phone, autofill three different sites.
  • For one critical account, sign out everywhere and sign back in with MFA.

Common pitfalls

  • Browser keeps saving new passwords. Turn the browser’s password saving off to avoid new duplicates.
  • Only one hardware key enrolled. Add two and label them.
  • Backup codes get lost. Store codes inside each item’s secure notes.

Privacy notes

  • Good managers encrypt on your device before sync. That means the provider cannot read your vault.
  • TOTP codes stored in the same manager are convenient. Storing TOTP on a separate authenticator or hardware key is stronger but less convenient. Choose based on risk.

Keep going

Next in the series: Browser hygiene that sticks without breaking your favorite sites.

  • Password Migration Checklist (PDF): Download
  • Top Ten Account Security Worksheet (CSV): Download

entry.title: WSUS just became an attacker’s dream. Stop publishing your patch pipeline to the internet.
entry.content:
When a patching platform turns into an initial-access vector, you are looking at failure stacked on failure. That is exactly what CVE-2025-59287 did for Windows Server Update Services (WSUS): an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw from unsafe deserialization, actively exploited in the wild, with an emergency out-of-band fix from Microsoft after the regular Patch Tuesday did not fully close the hole (Unit 42, 2025; TechRadar Pro, 2025). Translation for busy admins and business owners: the service you trust to keep Windows updated can be abused to run attacker code as SYSTEM.

As a security analyst working with small and midsize environments, I will be blunt. Too many WSUS servers are exposed to the open internet on 8530 and 8531. That is not modern IT. That is rolling out a welcome mat. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 observed live exploitation within hours of Microsoft’s emergency release, and external scans found thousands of exposed WSUS endpoints. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and told federal agencies to fix it on a deadline. When the government sets a date, the rest of us should read the room (Unit 42, 2025; Infosecurity Magazine, 2025; NIST NVD, 2025).

What this incident actually teaches

  1. Asset management and network design beat hero patching. If WSUS is reachable from the internet, a single mistake becomes an enterprise problem. Your patching tier belongs behind a VPN or private access broker, not on public IPs. Flat networks make every bug high impact.

  2. “We patched” is not a control. Microsoft’s first fix was incomplete. That happens. Compensating controls like strict ingress rules, TLS termination you control, and allow-listed admin paths would have reduced blast radius while you validated the out-of-band update (TechRadar Pro, 2025; ITPro, 2025).

  3. Logs are your truth serum. The early tradecraft is boring in the best way: parent processes from wsusservice.exe or w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe then powershell.exe, followed by quick recon and exfil to webhook collectors. If your EDR never flags that tree, do not call your detection program mature (Unit 42, 2025).

My playbook for SMB and mid market clients this week

  • Kill exposure first. If 8530 or 8531 is open to the world, close it. Use an access broker, private link, or at minimum source IP allow listing. Internet facing WSUS is a non starter.
  • Apply the out of band updates and reboot. Verify the right KB per server version and confirm the binary build after patch. Do not stop at Installed in Windows Update history. Cross check against the NVD entry and the vendor advisories for version coverage (NIST NVD, 2025; TechRadar Pro, 2025).
  • Hunt now, not next quarter. Query EDR for the specific process chains tied to WSUS service and IIS. Review IIS WSUSPool logs for unusual POSTs to cookie or reporting endpoints over the last 14 to 21 days. Treat any finding as potential lateral movement.
  • Segment and service bind. WSUS should only talk to domain members and Microsoft upstream. No east west free for all. Put it on its own VLAN with ACLs that match those facts.
  • Re evaluate WSUS as a pattern, not as a product. If your organization cannot safely run internet adjacent infrastructure, move to update models that reduce on prem attack surface, like Windows Update for Business or controlled cloud management, and keep on prem only when you can enforce private access and hard boundaries.
  • Turn this into tabletop fuel. Add core patch pipeline compromised to your incident response scenarios. Practice what you would do if the very system that distributes trust is hostile for a day.

Why this is a bigger story than one CVE

Ransomware crews want reliable paths to domain trust. A management tier that is reachable, under monitored, and running high privilege services gives them exactly that. We keep calling Zero Trust a strategy, then publish WSUS to the internet for convenience. That gap is where intrusions start.

If this stings a little, good. Security culture changes when something that always worked is finally seen as fragile. This month is the moment to retire habits that were fine in 2015 and indefensible in 2025.

References

Infosecurity Magazine. (2025, October 28). Actively exploited WSUS bug added to CISA KEV list. https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/actively-exploited-wsus-bug-cisa/

NIST National Vulnerability Database. (2025). CVE-2025-59287 detail. https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-59287

TechRadar Pro. (2025, October 24). Microsoft issues emergency Windows Server security patch. https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/microsoft-issues-emergency-windows-server-security-patch-update-now-or-risk-attack

TechRadar Pro. (2025, October 28). US government orders patching of critical Windows Server security issue. https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/us-government-orders-patching-of-critical-windows-server-security-issue

Unit 42. (2025, October 28). Microsoft WSUS Remote Code Execution (CVE-2025-59287) actively exploited in the wild [Threat brief]. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/microsoft-cve-2025-59287/

ITPro. (2025, October 27). CISA issues alert after botched Windows Server patch exposes critical flaw. https://www.itpro.com/security/cisa-issues-alert-after-botched-windows-server-patch-exposes-critical-flaw

Forbes. (2025, October 26). Act now: Microsoft issues emergency Windows update as attacks begin. https://www.forbes.com/sites/daveywinder/2025/10/26/act-now---microsoft-issues-emergency-windows-update-as-attacks-begin/

entry.title: Embedding Mastodon Posts in Eleventy: My Journey
entry.content:
I wanted a Mastodon status to sit inside an Eleventy post without breaking my layout or forcing weird fixed sizes. I tried the usual suspects and hit the same walls each time. In the end, a simple shortcode solved it. The page controls width and Mastodon’s script sets height. It also supports a full-bleed option when I want the embed to break out of the narrow reading column. That same general “make Mastodon fit the site cleanly” mindset also led me to build an Eleventy plugin for sharing posts to Mastodon later on.

This write-up documents what failed fast, what finally worked, and the exact code I am using now.

What I tried first

  • oEmbed or plugin output that injected an iframe with fixed width and height. Looked fine at one breakpoint, broke at others.
  • CSS overrides on the iframe. As soon as the script rerendered, my sizes lost.
  • Loading the iframe before the embed script. The first height message went missing, so the card stayed short.

The working approach

  • I control width with the container. Inside the prose column it uses the column width. In full-bleed mode it uses min(100vw, cap).
  • Mastodon controls height. No fixed height is set. Height is updated by embed.js via postMessage.
  • I load embed.js before the iframe so the listener is ready when the first message arrives.

Step 1: Add the shortcode to eleventy.js

Paste this function into your Eleventy config and register it. It guards against loading the script twice per origin and supports an optional bleed layout.

// Mastodon Direct-Embed: bleed-friendly, auto-height reliable
async function mastodonEmbedShortcode(statusUrl, maxWidth = 720, layout = 'normal') {
  try {
    const u = new URL(String(statusUrl));
    const embedSrc  = `${u.origin}${u.pathname}/embed";
    const scriptSrc = `${u.origin}/embed.js`;
    const w = Math.max(1, Number(maxWidth) || 720);
    const bleed = String(layout).toLowerCase() === 'bleed';

    // Wrapper: normal uses a capped box; bleed escapes the prose column and centers content
    const wrapperStyle = bleed
      ? `style="width:100vw; position:relative; left:50%; right:50%; margin-left:-50vw; margin-right:-50vw; display:grid; place-items:center;"`
      : `style="max-width:${w}px; margin:0 auto;"`;

    // Iframe: do not fix height; let embed.js resize it. Give a small min-height to avoid a flash.
    const iframeStyle = bleed
      ? `style="width:min(100vw, ${w}px); border:0; display:block; overflow:hidden; min-height:300px;"`
      : `style="width:100%; border:0; display:block; overflow:hidden; min-height:300px;"`;

    // Load embed.js first (non-async), once per origin
    const loaderId = `masto-embed-loader-${u.origin.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '')}`;
    const loader = \`
<script>
  (function(id, src){
    if (!document.getElementById(id)) {
      var s = document.createElement('script');
      s.id = id; s.src = '\${scriptSrc}';
      document.head.appendChild(s);
    }
  })('\${loaderId}', '\${scriptSrc}');
</script>\`.trim();

    return \`
\${loader}
<div class="mastodon-embed-wrapper" \${wrapperStyle}>
  <iframe
    class="mastodon-embed"
    src="\${embedSrc}"
    \${iframeStyle}
    sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-popups"
    allow="fullscreen"
    loading="lazy"
  ></iframe>
</div>\`.trim();

  } catch {
    return \`<p><a href="\${statusUrl}">\${statusUrl}</a></p>\`;
  }
}

// Register for all template engines you use
eleventyConfig.addNunjucksAsyncShortcode('mastodon', mastodonEmbedShortcode);
eleventyConfig.addLiquidShortcode('mastodon', (url, w, layout) => mastodonEmbedShortcode(url, w, layout));
eleventyConfig.addJavaScriptFunction('mastodon', mastodonEmbedShortcode);

Step 2: Use it in content

Inside the regular reading column:

{% mastodon "https://mastodon.social/@deejayy/115454110249651937" %}

Full-bleed across the viewport, capped at 720:

{% mastodon "https://mastodon.social/@deejayy/115454110249651937", 720, "bleed" %}

Result

Here is how the embed would look on your page:

Regular width: (Infosec.exchange)

Full-bleed:

Test with another instance: (Vivaldi Social)

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • If the height never adjusts, check for a global CSS rule that forces iframe { height: ... !important }.
  • Make sure your Content Security Policy allows <instance>/embed.js.
  • Ad blockers can sometimes block the script. Allow it.
  • If you use multiple Mastodon instances on one page, this loader only injects one script per origin.

Why I skipped plugins this time

I like batteries-included tools, but the layout rules in my theme are opinionated. A small shortcode gave me reliable control over width while letting Mastodon handle height correctly. Less glue, fewer surprises.

References

  • Eleventy Plugin: Embed Everything
    https://gfscott.com/embed-everything/
  • eleventy-plugin-embed-everything (npm)
    https://www.npmjs.com/package/eleventy-plugin-embed-everything
  • eleventy-plugin-embed-mastodon (npm)
    https://www.npmjs.com/package/eleventy-plugin-embed-mastodon
  • Andy Piper — Mastodon oEmbed examples
    https://andypiper.org/mastodon-embeds-examples/single-post-oembed.html

entry.title: Remove Preinstalled Microsoft Store Apps in Windows 11 (24H2 & 25H2)
entry.content:
last updated on October 29, 2025

Update October 29, 2025:
@deejayy over on Mastodon brought to my attention a great Powershell script that also removes all the bloatware from > > Windows 11. Check it out on Github. I have given this a try and it works great!

For new user profiles, existing users, and at-scale management with Intune

Windows 11 ships with a pile of inbox Microsoft Store apps. Some are useful, others add noise. This guide shows you how to remove them the right way:

  • clean up what new profiles get by default
  • clean up existing users
  • roll the change out with Intune, CSP, or GPO on Windows 11 Enterprise and Education 25H2+

Microsoft now supports a policy-based removal that deprovisions selected inbox apps, so you can stop babysitting brittle scripts.

What this feature does and does not do

  • Scope: Removes selected Microsoft-provisioned Store apps. It does not remove third-party OEM utilities.
  • Timing: Runs at OOBE, at user sign-in after an OS upgrade, or after policy changes. Existing users keep apps until sign out/in after the policy is applied.
  • Supported editions: Windows 11 Enterprise and Education on 25H2+ for the policy method. Windows 11 Pro still requires deprovisioning or imaging techniques.
  • Reinstall behavior: While removal is selected, Windows blocks reinstall from the Store until you flip the app back to “False” and reprovision or reinstall it.

Quick reference: approaches in this article

  • GPO / Intune policy (25H2 ENT/EDU): best for new profiles at scale
  • Registry (ADMX-backed keys): same policy under the hood, useful for testing or automation
  • PowerShell per-user removal: cleans the signed-in user now
  • PowerShell or DISM deprovision: prevents apps from installing for future users on a device or image

Method 1 — Remove apps with Group Policy (good for small pilots)

  1. Open Local Group Policy Editor or create a domain GPO.
  2. Go to:
    Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → App Package Deployment
  3. Open Remove default Microsoft Store packages from the system and set to Enabled.
  4. Pick the apps to remove and apply.
  5. Test with a new user profile or sign out/in after policy arrives.

Verify on a client: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Appx\RemoveDefaultMicrosoftStorePackages contains values for selected apps.

Method 2 — Remove apps with Intune (Settings Catalog or OMA-URI)

Settings Catalog

  • Create a Device configuration profile in Intune.
  • Category: Administrative Templates → Windows Components → App Package Deployment
  • Setting: Remove default Microsoft Store packages from the system = Enabled
  • Toggle True per app and assign to device groups. Unsupported devices show Not applicable.

OMA-URI (ADMX-backed CSP)

  • Path:
    ./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/ApplicationManagement/RemoveDefaultMicrosoftStorePackages
  • Data type: String
  • Value: XML payload like the example below. Use true to remove, false to keep.
<enabled/>
<data id="MicrosoftStickyNotes" value="true"/>
<data id="MicrosoftSolitaireCollection" value="true"/>
<data id="BingNews" value="true"/>
<data id="BingWeather" value="true"/>
<data id="GamingApp" value="true"/>
<data id="XboxGamingOverlay" value="true"/>
<data id="XboxIdentityProvider" value="true"/>
<data id="XboxSpeechToTextOverlay" value="true"/>
<data id="XboxTCUI" value="true"/>

<!-- Common keepers in enterprise images -->
<data id="WindowsCalculator" value="false"/>
<data id="WindowsCamera" value="false"/>
<data id="WindowsNotepad" value="false"/>
<data id="Paint" value="false"/>
<data id="Photos" value="false"/>
<data id="QuickAssist" value="false"/>
<data id="WindowsTerminal" value="false"/>
<data id="MediaPlayer" value="false"/>
<data id="OutlookForWindows" value="false"/>
<data id="MSTeams" value="false"/>

Intune’s native UI can lag the Windows release. If you do not see the setting yet, use the OMA-URI method as a temporary path.

Method 3 — Apply the policy via registry (useful for tests and automation)

The policy writes under:
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Appx\RemoveDefaultMicrosoftStorePackages

  • Enabled = 1
  • Create a subkey per app and mark it for removal (ADMX-backed policy structure).

Admins often seed these keys with a script during imaging or break-glass scenarios, then migrate to Intune or GPO for long-term control.

Method 4 — Clean up existing users now (PowerShell)

Policy focuses on what new profiles get. To clean up users who are already logged in, remove their installed copies and then deprovision so the apps do not return.

<#
Removes selected Store apps for all existing users,
then deprovisions those apps so NEW users will not get them.
Run as admin.
#>

$Patterns = @(
  '*MicrosoftStickyNotes*',
  '*Microsoft.MicrosoftSolitaireCollection*',
  '*Microsoft.BingNews*',
  '*Microsoft.BingWeather*',
  '*Microsoft.GamingApp*',
  '*Microsoft.XboxGamingOverlay*',
  '*Microsoft.XboxIdentityProvider*',
  '*Microsoft.XboxSpeechToTextOverlay*',
  '*Microsoft.Xbox.TCUI*'
)

Write-Host 'Phase 1: remove from existing users'
foreach ($pat in $Patterns) {
  Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name $pat -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    ForEach-Object {
      try {
        Write-Host "Removing per-user: $($_.Name)"
        Remove-AppxPackage -Package $($_.PackageFullName) -AllUsers -ErrorAction Stop
      } catch {
        Write-Warning "Failed removing $($_.Name): $($_.Exception.Message)"
      }
    }
}

Write-Host 'Phase 2: deprovision so new users do not get them'
$prov = Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online
foreach ($pat in $Patterns) {
  $prov | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like $pat -or $_.PackageName -like $pat } |
    ForEach-Object {
      try {
        Write-Host "Deprovisioning: $($_.DisplayName)"
        Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online -PackageName $($_.PackageName) | Out-Null
      } catch {
        Write-Warning "Failed deprovisioning $($_.DisplayName): $($_.Exception.Message)"
      }
    }
}
  • Remove-AppxPackage removes per-user copies.
  • Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage edits the device’s provisioning template for future profiles.

Method 5 — Service an image with DISM (offline or online)

For gold images or break-glass CLI:

dism /Online /Get-ProvisionedAppxPackages
dism /Online /Remove-ProvisionedAppxPackage /PackageName:<PackageName>

Same effect as the PowerShell deprovision cmdlet, via DISM.

Troubleshooting and verification

  • Event Viewer: Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → AppxDeployment-Server → Operational
    Watch for Event IDs 762 (removed), 606 (skipped due to policy), 614 (failed).
  • Registry check: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Appx\RemoveDefaultMicrosoftStorePackages has app subkeys and values when the policy is active.
  • Intune status: Device configuration profile shows Succeeded for supported devices, Not applicable otherwise.
  • Sysprep and upgrades: If you tinker with provisioned apps manually, Sysprep can complain. Standardize on one method to avoid surprises.

FAQ

Which apps can I remove with the policy?
Microsoft provides a curated list that currently includes Calculator, Camera, Photos, Sticky Notes, Solitaire, Teams, Outlook for Windows, Notepad, Paint, Quick Assist, Sound Recorder, Windows Terminal, Windows Media Player, and several Xbox components. The list can change over time.

Will this work on Windows 11 Pro?
The new removal policy targets Enterprise and Education on 25H2+. For Pro devices, use deprovisioning or image servicing.

Do I need both GPO and Intune?
No. Pick one channel per device to avoid conflicts.

Sources and further reading

  • Microsoft Tech Community announcement: Policy-based removal of pre-installed Microsoft Store apps
    https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windows-itpro-blog/policy-based-removal-of-pre-installed-microsoft-store-apps/4463835

  • Microsoft Learn — Policy-based inbox app removal (Intune, CSP, GPO, timing, event IDs, XML)
    https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/configuration/policy-based-inbox-app-removal

  • PowerShell: Remove-AppxPackage (per-user removal)
    https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/appx/remove-appxpackage

  • PowerShell: Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage (deprovision for new profiles)
    https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/dism/remove-appxprovisionedpackage

  • DISM App Package servicing options
    https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/dism-app-package--appx-or-msix--servicing-command-line-options

  • Reference style you liked for context (similar structure, not a source of commands):
    https://www.tech2geek.net/how-to-remove-preinstalled-microsoft-store-apps-in-windows-11-24h2-25h2-for-new-user-profiles/

entry.title: Weekly Notes: Week 43, 2025
entry.content:
Last week was a crazy ride in my personal life. Here are my notes for the week.

💻 Work

I only worked two days. I took Wednesday through Friday off to handle personal matters (more on that below). The short week in the office was calm for a change, which I appreciated after the chaos before. I cleared out emails and knocked out a stack of small tasks that had been waiting.

😎 Personal

I took a few days off for family health issues. On Wednesday, my mom was sent to the ER after an abnormal EKG at her appointment. My dad struggles with the medical details, so I drove over to help. By the time I arrived, they had tried medication to stabilize her heart rate and rhythm, but it was not working as hoped. They had to cardiovert her to restore a normal rhythm. She stayed overnight for observation and more tests.

Thursday, I had already planned to take my dad to his out-of-town appointment. After we returned, I visited my mom at the hospital. The team continued testing, including an echocardiogram and a stress test. They determined she had a prior heart attack at some point, though the timing is unclear. They want to do a scope, but are weighing timing because of her kidney issues. As of now, she is still in the hospital.

🎾 Last Tennis Tournament

Saturday was supposed to be the final tournament of the season. Check-in was 7:45 a.m. for an 8:30 start. It rained off and on the night before, and while the rain had stopped by morning, the courts were wet. They delayed the start and rolled the courts, but the cloudy, humid weather slowed the drying. Play began on half the courts after about an hour, and within 25 minutes it started sprinkling again. They called the tournament, and not even one full match was completed. I was disappointed, especially since my daughter missed the previous tournament and this one was canceled. There is always next season.

📝 Articles

With all that was going on last week, I really didn’t get much articles written. I did though launch my new Discord community which I am super excited about. Here is the article I wrote highlighting it.

  • The CybersecKyle Community is live: security and tech, together

That is it for this week. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

entry.title: The CybersecKyle Community is live: security and tech, together
entry.content:
Update December 12, 2025: The CyberTech Guild Community has been suset. I want to thank everyone who joined, contributed, and helped build a welcoming space over the past two years. If you are looking for similar communities, I recommend checking out AllThingsTech if you’re looking for a great technology focused server. Or Owlsec for those more Cybersecursity minded.

After weeks of planning, testing, and building, I am excited to open the doors to the CybersecKyle Community, a Discord space for people who care about security and technology in equal measure. It is for beginners learning the ropes, students and career changers building momentum, and experienced folks who enjoy trading notes and sharpening their craft.

Why both security and tech?

Security does not live in a vacuum. The best defenses grow out of sound engineering, good automation, clear documentation, and a healthy respect for how people really use systems. Likewise, great tech work benefits from a security mindset that thinks about failure modes, data privacy, resilience, and recovery. This community blends the two so you do not have to learn them apart.

What you will find inside

Security and infosec tracks

  • News and threat analysis: Daily headlines, notable CVEs, and practical ways to reduce risk
  • Blue team practice: Logging that pays off, detection ideas, tabletop prompts, incident response drills
  • Red and purple topics: Legal and ethical methodology, emulation ideas that help defenders learn
  • Privacy and governance: Consent, data minimization, policy that people can follow

Tech and engineering tracks

  • Systems and cloud: Linux tips, Windows hardening without the headache, AWS and Azure basics to advanced IAM
  • Automation: Scripting with Bash or PowerShell, GitHub Actions, useful one-liners that save real time
  • Dev and tooling: Editors and IDEs, CLI tricks, containers, local lab setups, performance tuning
  • Productivity and setups: Hardware talk, dotfiles, shortcuts, clean workflows that reduce friction

Crossover spaces

  • Secure architecture reviews: Tradeoffs in the open
  • Build-and-break labs: Try something, measure the result, write it up
  • Career and certifications: Study groups, resume feedback, mock interview questions
  • Tech talk and chill: Coffee chats, music, memes, and general hangouts

You will also see blog updates from me so we can discuss new posts in context. Cyber News and Tech News from various sources will be shared regularly to keep everyone informed.

Who this is for

  • Beginners: Safe questions and patient explanations with links to labs that actually work
  • Intermediate members: Space to compare tools, share configs, and practice tradeoffs
  • Advanced practitioners: Room for nuance, architecture discussions, and deep dives
  • The simply curious: Digital hygiene tips, app safety, and news summaries in plain language

What “cyber” means here

  • Defense first: Patch with intent, back up with purpose, monitor what matters, practice recovery
  • Privacy by default: Smaller data footprints and clear permission boundaries
  • Evidence over hype: Reproduce results, measure impact, share what you learned
  • Teach as you go: If you fix a problem, leave a note someone else can use tomorrow

Culture and conduct

  • Kind, direct, and helpful: Ask in good faith, answer with patience, cite when useful
  • Ethical boundaries: Research and testing only on systems you own or have permission to use
  • Zero gatekeeping: Everyone starts somewhere, everyone teaches something
  • Signal over noise: Share tools and tactics you have actually touched

How to jump in

  1. Join the server:
  2. Read the welcome, skim the rules, say hello
  3. Pick a couple of channels that match your interests
  4. Post one small thing you learned this week or one thing you want to learn next

A final word

Security is stronger when it grows beside good engineering. Tech is better when it carries a security mindset from the start. If you want a place where people build, learn, and look out for each other, you will feel at home here. Bring curiosity, bring questions, bring small improvements. We will make steady progress together. A community is only as strong as its members, and I can’t wait to see what we build. You can also help shape this community by inviting others you know who would benefit. Let’s grow together!

entry.title: Weekly Notes: Week 42, 2025
entry.content:
Last week was one heck of a week at work. Very stressful which bleed into my personal life which I never like. Add all this up and this was a week that I am glad is over. Here are my notes for the week.

💻 Work

Let’s start off with work since that was the most stressful part of my week. I won’t go into too much of the detail or rewrite it all, you can find the full story on my Mastodon post here. But, long story short, a third-party vendor one of our clients use for their dealership that connects their printers to the vendors DMS system, rermoved all of the printers from both of the clients locations. They were unable to print anything from this system. This was a huge problem since this system is used to print all of the paperwork for the vehicles they sell. This included everything from the buyer’s order, to the title work, to the registration forms, to the financing documents, and more.

In total, I spent about 3 days getting this set all back up and running. It was a total nightmare.

😎 Personal

As I mentioned earlier, work stress spilled over into my personal life this week. My mood was off most of the time, and I felt tense and generally unhappy. I tried to stay composed for my family, but it wasn’t easy. I hate when that happens because it’s not their fault, and it feels unfair to let my frustration affect them. I’m relieved the week is behind me and hopeful for a clean slate ahead.

Over the weekend, there was supposed to be a tennis tournament, my daughter’s first, but I found out she told her coach she wouldn’t be there because it conflicted with her choir regional tryout. She technically could have done both since it was an open tournament, but she chose not to. I was a bit disappointed, especially since I’d been looking forward to her first tournament.

🏎️ F1

This past weekend was the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, one of the tracks on my bucket list to visit. It marked Round 19 of the 2025 F1 season, and we’re getting close to the finish line. The race was exciting to watch, though not without some disappointment. With it being a Sprint weekend, Oscar (one of my favorite drivers, by the way) had two chances to pick up more points and extend his lead in the drivers’ championship, but things didn’t go as planned. The sprint race ended in disaster with a DNF and Max taking the win, and the Grand Prix wrapped up with Max winning again while Oscar finished in P5. Still, any weekend that includes F1 is a good weekend in my book.

📝 Articles

I was a little slow on my writing last week. Here were the articles I wrote.

  • Cybersecurity Weekly Roundup for October 11–17, 2025
  • Sora, Hands-On: thrilling for creators, thorny for privacy

That is it for this week. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

entry.title: Sora, Hands-On: thrilling for creators, thorny for privacy
entry.content:
Sora is both interesting and scary. Interesting because it lets anyone direct short, realistic videos with synced audio on a phone. Scary because it turns identity itself into a shareable asset other people can cast. Those two truths sit together in one app.

OpenAI says Sora 2 improves realism, physics, and instruction following, and it ships inside a social app that is rolling out now in the United States and Canada. Downloads include a visible moving watermark and C2PA provenance metadata to signal that a clip was generated by Sora. That is a stronger baseline than most consumer tools so far (OpenAI: “Sora 2 is here”; Sora landing; Launching Sora responsibly; Getting started guide).

What Sora does in practice

  • Short, directed clips with audio. You write a prompt with camera hints and timing. Sora renders a 10–15 second video with synchronized sound and natural motion. OpenAI’s system card and launch post emphasize better physics and steerability compared with earlier models (System card; Sora 2 announcement).
  • Cameos of real people. This is the headline feature. You record a selfie capture to create a reusable, permissioned “cameo” of yourself that can be cast by others you allow (Cameo help).
  • Provenance signals. Sora adds a visible moving watermark and embeds C2PA credentials in the file to help downstream verification. C2PA is the open standard for content authenticity metadata and is being adopted across cameras, newsrooms, and AI tools (Launching responsibly; Getting started; C2PA explainer).

Cameos: the best feature and the riskiest concept

You can control who is allowed to feature your cameo:

  • Only me
  • People I approve
  • Mutuals
  • Everyone

You can also set Cameo rules, review drafts that include you, revoke access going forward, and remove videos that use your cameo. Teen accounts are limited to stricter settings by default (Cameo help; Getting started).

The consent model is better than the free-for-all deepfake scene, but there is still social risk. You do not pre-approve each individual video before someone generates it. You can delete or report afterward, yet someone may have seen or screen-recorded it already. Reporting from reviewers highlights exactly this dynamic: it feels fun until a friend uses your face in a way you did not expect, then you realize the guardrails are reactive rather than preventive (Washington Post analysis).

Guardrails, public figures, and the moving policy line

OpenAI claims it blocks depictions of public figures unless those people opt in through cameo. The company has also said it is working with rightsholders for more granular control over copyrighted characters (Launching responsibly). Reality is evolving in public. After a wave of controversial videos of deceased figures, OpenAI paused depictions of Martin Luther King Jr. and said estates of other figures can request an opt-out. This is a live example of how safety policy is adjusting to real misuse pressure in days, not months (Business Insider; Forbes; The Verge).

Other reporting has examined Sora’s ability to mimic popular formats and styles, raising questions about training data, rightsholder control, and accountability once videos begin to spread across platforms (Washington Post training-data investigation).

The infosec angle: what changes when Sora goes mainstream

Think of Sora as a deepfake pipeline that regular people will actually use. That shift matters more than any single model metric. Here is how the threat model changes.

1) Identity and reputation attacks get easier to stage

Highly believable short clips of a co-worker, candidate, or journalist can be made quickly with their own consented cameo or with a convincing look-alike if you try to skirt rules. Family members of deceased celebrities are already reporting harm and harassment from viral Sora videos, which is a canary for reputational attacks in other contexts (Washington Post report on dead-celebrity videos).

Practical response: write a short synthetic-media policy. Define how your team labels AI video, what to do when a malicious clip appears, and who confirms authenticity before any public comment.

2) Watermarks help but do not absolve

Visible marks can be cropped or obscured in re-uploads. C2PA helps when you have the original file, but many social platforms still strip or mangle metadata during transcode. Treat provenance as a necessary verification step, not a guarantee that the public will see the signal in feeds (Launching responsibly; C2PA explainer).

Practical response: keep master copies with credentials intact. Use C2PA-aware tools to verify when possible. Publish originals from your own domain or platform that preserves credentials, then reference that canonical copy when rumors start.

3) Social engineering content will upgrade fast

Sora can output short, “native” vertical clips with audio that feel like platform content. Expect more convincing vishing pretexts, fake executive messages, and crisis videos.

Practical response: train on real vs. Sora examples. Teach people to trust source and provenance over vibes. Incorporate Sora-style prompts into red-team scenarios.

4) Consent friction is real, even with options

Cameo privacy settings let you choose Only me, People I approve, Mutuals, or Everyone. They are good defaults, but they rely on users to curate allow-lists and revoke access quickly when something goes sideways. Reviewers have already shown the gap between “I can remove it later” and “damage is done” (Cameo help; Washington Post analysis).

Practical response: default to Only me while you learn the app. Move to People I approve only for specific collaborators. Refresh the allow-list regularly. Add simple cameo rules in plain language so expectations are baked into the asset.

5) Policy will keep shifting

The MLK pause shows how quickly OpenAI will adjust settings when harm becomes obvious, and it shows how public figures and estates will press for stronger veto power over likeness. Expect more toggles and special-case enforcement as rightsholders negotiate what “consent” means at platform scale (Business Insider; The Verge).

Practical response: do not assume today’s moderation results will match tomorrow’s. When you document risk, acknowledge that model behavior and policy may change mid-campaign.

What it is like to actually use Sora

From a creator’s chair, Sora works best when you give it clear, short direction and two or three beats per clip. Lip sync and micro-expressions are surprisingly personal with cameo recordings. Crowded scenes and very fast camera moves still stumble, which matches OpenAI’s own notes on known limitations (Sora 2 announcement; System card).

Recommendations for teams, schools, and civil organizations

  1. Publish an authenticity policy
    Promise to disclose when a video is AI-generated, and explain your verification steps when debunking a fake.

  2. Use provenance end to end
    Keep originals with C2PA. Host a canonical copy where credentials survive. When posting elsewhere, point back to that source (C2PA explainer).

  3. Run a synthetic-media drill
    Scenario: a fake video of your spokesperson starts circulating. Who verifies, who responds, and where will you post the canonical correction?

  4. Cameo hygiene
    Default to Only me. If you open to People I approve, keep the list tight and review it monthly. Add Cameo rules that forbid sensitive topics or political themes (Cameo help).

  5. Track policy changes
    Subscribe to official updates and credible tech press. The MLK pause is not the last adjustment you will see (Launching responsibly; Business Insider).

Where this leaves us

Sora is a creative rocket and a reputational risk amplifier. The watermark and C2PA story is a meaningful start, not a shield. The cameo system gives consent levers we have not had before in consumer video tools, yet consent still collides with virality. If you create with Sora, build provenance into your workflow and publish with context. If you protect people or brands, assume Sora-quality fakes are already part of your threat model.

entry.title: Cybersecurity Weekly Roundup for October 11–17, 2025
entry.content:
🧭 Overview

The last seven days were busy: Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday shipped a heavy set of fixes, CISA issued an emergency directive on F5 gear, Oracle E-Business Suite attacks spilled into aviation, Qantas customer data hit the wild, and Cisco network devices saw post-patch exploitation. Healthcare and higher-ed continue to take hits, while Europe logged a notable cybercrime takedown. Here’s the signal, minus the noise.

1️⃣ Microsoft Patch Tuesday lands with actively exploited bugs

Microsoft’s October update fixed a large set of CVEs, including multiple zero-days under active exploitation. Priorities tilt toward Windows privilege escalation and remote code execution. Triage domain controllers, RAS/VPN, and edge-exposed workloads first.

Practitioner take: Patch DCs and RAS servers before endpoints. Hunt for privilege-escalation chains in EDR and RasMan anomalies.

2️⃣ CISA issues emergency directive after F5 breach

Following a breach at F5 that included theft of source code and internal vulnerability info, CISA ordered federal agencies to rapidly patch or replace affected BIG-IP and BIG-IQ families. Reporting points to a nation-state actor and broader supply-chain risk.

Practitioner take: Inventory every F5 device by version and exposure. If internet-facing, assume credential risk and rotate associated secrets.

3️⃣ Oracle E-Business Suite exploitation hits aviation (Envoy Air)

Envoy Air confirmed an intrusion tied to Oracle E-Business Suite exploitation and extortion-style pressure, with no flight operations impact reported. Oracle pushed fixes as attacks ramped.

Practitioner take: Validate EBS patch levels and SSO integrations. Review service accounts and outbound EBS traffic for oddities.

4️⃣ Qantas customer data leaked after earlier breach

Qantas said data stolen months ago has now been leaked, affecting millions of flyers and elevating phishing risk. Exposed data includes contact and loyalty information.

Practitioner take: Expect airline-themed lures. Add temporary MFA friction for at-risk cohorts and warn frequent-flyer travelers.

5️⃣ Adobe AEM flaw added to CISA KEV

CISA added an actively exploited Adobe Experience Manager Forms vulnerability to the Known Exploited list. Public proof-of-concept code exists for related AEM issues and agencies have a near-term patch deadline.

Practitioner take: Patch AEM now. Review WAF rules and hunt for unusual author or publish activity and any webshell indicators.

6️⃣ Cisco IOS and IOS XE SNMP bug exploited to plant rootkits

Researchers detailed a campaign where threat actors used a Cisco SNMP vulnerability to deploy persistent Linux rootkits on network devices. Cisco previously warned of active exploitation.

Practitioner take: Patch network OS images and disable legacy SNMP where possible. Inspect for unexpected processes, modified boot variables, or integrity check failures.

7️⃣ Healthcare: multiple providers disclose incidents

U.S. providers continued breach notifications this week, underscoring sustained attacker pressure on regional healthcare.

Practitioner take: Lock down vendor access, prune stale SFTP and VPN accounts, and test immutable backups with a real restore.

8️⃣ U.K. NCSC Annual Review flags surge in nationally significant attacks

The U.K. cybersecurity authority logged a record rise in nationally significant incidents year over year, with ransomware still a prime mover.

Practitioner take: Treat ransomware as a reliability risk. Invest in configuration baselines, tested restores, and access hygiene.

9️⃣ Higher-ed breach fallout: University of St. Thomas case study

Reporting on the University of St. Thomas breach shows large volumes of sensitive data exposed and slow notification cycles, a pattern common in cash-strapped higher-ed.

Practitioner take: Map where PII actually lives, reduce retention, and pre-write comms playbooks to avoid delays when it matters.

🔟 Europol arrests seven in cross-border cybercrime operation

Europol coordinated arrests and seizures across Europe, dismantling a fraud operation with millions in losses and extensive SIM-box infrastructure.

Practitioner take: Expect short-term actor churn, not a drop in fraud. Keep telecom and OTP-bypass detections warm.

🧠 Key Takeaway

Identity and edge are the pressure points. Patch the gear that brokers trust — F5, AEM, Cisco — shore up Windows privilege paths, and assume data-rich platforms will be phished. Configuration discipline, tested restores, and aggressive vendor hygiene are the fastest ways to buy down risk this month.

🔗 References

  1. Microsoft Patch Tuesday — 172 flaws, six zero-days (Oct 14, 2025). BleepingComputer Also: CrowdStrike analysis and Petri coverage

  2. CISA Emergency Directive 26-01 on F5 after source-code theft. WSJ, TechRadar Pro, FedRAMP note Background: The Hacker News.

  3. Envoy Air breach tied to Oracle E-Business Suite exploitation. Reuters, The Record, BleepingComputer

  4. Qantas customer data leak following Salesforce-linked intrusion. The Guardian, Outpost24, SalesforceBen

  5. Adobe AEM Forms CVE-2025-54253 added to CISA KEV (patch by Nov 5). CISA KEV alert and KEV catalog entry; analysis: The Hacker News.

  6. Cisco IOS/IOS XE SNMP CVE-2025-20352 used to plant rootkits (“Operation Zero Disco”). Trend Micro Research; summary: The Hacker News

  7. Health sector: continuing breach pressure and sector advisories. HHS HC3 products hub and OCR breach portal. HC3, OCR breach portal

  8. U.K. NCSC Annual Review 2025 — rise in nationally significant incidents. The Guardian, overview recap: Technology Magazine.

  9. University of St. Thomas breach reporting (higher-ed case). ABC13/Houston Chronicle recap

  10. Europol-coordinated takedown — 7 arrests, SIM-box infrastructure seized (Oct 10 op, announced Oct 17). Europol newsroom item; coverage: Euronews and CyberScoop
